hn.title: Ask HN: How did you convince family and friends to join your XMPP/Matrix server?
hn.text: I love open-source software and open protocols, but my family and friends primarily communicate through SMS for exactly the reasons in https://xkcd.com/2365/ Whenever XMPP or Matrix threads pop up on HN, several commenters casually mention their "friends and family XMPP (or Matrix) server." How did you convince friends and family to move away from SMS/WhatsApp and replace it with a niche messaging app? My family and friends aren't hardcore nerdy, but they're more tech-savvy than average. Their needs in messaging are mainly pragmatic: they want ease of use, reliability, and fun features. They don't care that much about privacy, decentralization, or extensibility (though I care about those things a lot). I've been experimenting with self-hosting XMPP and Matrix servers and clients in the past week, and the UX is even worse than I expected. It seems like all the clients either imitate Slack, imitate Discord, or imitate hot garbage. I haven't seen any that try to be a simple, friendly replacement for SMS. I'm a software developer who uses computers all day, and I find the UX for most of the clients incredibly hard to use. The only angle I could see to pitch XMPP/Matrix to people for non-philosophical reasons are that there's a more consistent experience across iOS/Android. The biggest shortcoming I think is visible to regular users is that there's feature degradation and missing information when iOS users have SMS conversations with Android users, especially in group chats. For people who have successfully won family and friends to XMPP or Matrix, what was your pitch? What do you recommend others do to make XMPP or Matrix an attractive experience for a regular person?

hn.title: Greece has its own Pompeii: Thera buried Akrotiri in ash 17th-16th century BCE
hn.text:
The ruins of Akrotiri, a Bronze Age settlement on what is now the Greek island of Santorini
Westend61 via Getty Images
The earth rumbled for days. Inhabitants of the seafaring Bronze Age settlement of Akrotiri watched smoke plume from Thera , a long-dormant volcano on what is now the Greek island of Santorini . People gathered their belongings and safely stored the valuables they were forced to leave behind. Then they fled by boat to nearby islands.
When these minor earthquakes and eruptions subsided, residents returned to Akrotiri, collecting materials for reconstruction and beginning the arduous process of repairing the damage . But the ground continued to tremble. As conditions worsened , they made the difficult decision to flee once more, hopeful that their homes would survive the coming devastation.
When Thera erupted again, the explosion was so powerful that it destroyed Akrotiri, burying the settlement (and the island that shared the volcano’s name) in some 200 feet of ash and pumice stone. The timing of the disaster is the subject of intense debate , but scholars generally date it to between 1620 and 1530 B.C.E. The event was one of the largest volcanic eruptions in recorded history: Thera released about four times more volcanic material than the infamous Krakatau eruption, which killed upwards of 36,000 people in what is now Indonesia in 1883.
A 2000 satellite image of Santorini. The bay at the center of the island is the volcanic caldera created by Thera's eruption.
Public domain via Wikimedia Commons
The fallout of the Thera eruption
The ash cloud formed by the Thera eruption completely transformed the island’s lush, humid environment into an arid one. Ash from the volcano was so widespread that it rained down as far as modern-day Egypt and Israel. Layers of sand and pebbles found between archaeological deposits suggest that multiple tsunamis also contributed to the destruction.
But the biggest fallout of this cataclysmic event happened when a portion of the volcanic caldera collapsed into the sea a few days after the eruption, forever changing the landscape of Santorini. This plummet into the depths of the Aegean Sea has become the stuff of legends . Some claim that Akrotiri is the lost city of Atlantis , which the Greek philosopher Plato described centuries later, around 360 B.C.E. Most modern scholars, however, agree that Plato created the tale of the sunken island as an allegorical device.
Did you know? The legend of Atlantis
In Plato’s telling, Atlantis was home to descendants of the sea god Poseidon , who turned on his progeny after they proved unworthy of his favor. According to the London-based Horniman Museum & Gardens , “The tale warns against the dangers of power and corruption, as well as stressing the importance of goodness.”
Plato’s Timaeus suggests that Atlantis succumbed to “violent earthquakes and floods, and in a single day of misfortune,” the island “disappeared in the depths of the sea.”
Much like the Roman city of Pompeii , which was destroyed when Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 C.E. , Akrotiri was preserved beneath the ash. “Everything was absolutely annihilated and completely encapsulated on the island,” says Lefteris Zorzos , an archaeologist whose research focuses on the prehistoric landscape of Santorini. This created a rare time capsule that provides an unprecedented look into the daily life of this Middle Bronze Age Cycladic civilization , so called after the Aegean islands where the culture flourished between about 3000 and 1000 B.C.E.
Santorini remained uninhabited for some 700 years . According to the ancient Greek historian Herodotus , Phoenicians started repopulating the island in the ninth century B.C.E. But more than 2,500 years would pass before archaeologists uncovered the ruins of ancient Akrotiri beneath the layers of dirt and ash.
Discovering Akrotiri
In 1866, miners working in pumice quarries on the island of Therasia , directly west of Thera, discovered a prehistoric building while collecting ash to insulate the Suez Canal . The French School at Athens launched a small excavation of the area in 1870, but a large-scale dig at Akrotiri only commenced nearly a century later, in 1967 , under the leadership of archaeologist Spyridon Marinatos .
A map of Bronze Age Thera, the Cyclades, Crete and the Peloponnese / Illustration by Meilan Solly
Marinatos had previously studied the excavated ruins of the Minoan Palace of Knossos in Crete, tracing pumice found on the island, some 74 miles south of Santorini, to the Thera eruption. His research marked the first time that the destruction of Akrotiri was directly linked to the decline of the Minoans , who are often identified as Europe’s first advanced civilization.
Marinatos posited that the earthquakes from Thera were so widespread, they toppled buildings and palaces on Crete. He also suggested that the resulting tsunamis damaged Minoan coastal settlements and halted shipping trade. But this theory is no longer widely accepted, and many historians now believe that the Minoans’ decline can’t be attributed to a single factor . Instead, they point to a combination of environmental changes, declining trade, political instability and conflicts with the ascendant Mycenean civilization .
Preserving an ancient site that was found remarkably intact presented a unique challenge for Marinatos. “When you excavate, you’re destroying a layer, removing the earth that’s keeping it all together,” Zorzos says. “You have to deal with this differently than you would a site that’s not as well preserved.” Before Marinatos could proceed, he had to build a shelter atop the ruins so they wouldn’t crumble when exposed to the elements.
Archaeologist Spyridon Marinatos photographs objects excavated on the island of Santorini, circa 1970
ullstein bild via Getty Images
Under the leadership of Marinatos and his successor, Christos Doumas , archaeologists have excavated sites across Akrotiri down to the bedrock, allowing scientist

hn.title: The Components of Agent Memory
hn.text:
Søren Kierkegaard wrote that life can only be understood backward , but it must be lived forward . We’ve encountered a similar bind when designing memory for AI agents.
As humans, we encode memory constantly as we go about our lives. The hippocampus plays a central role in this, capturing experiences in the moment so that memories form quickly and are immediately available. But only some experiences are consolidated into long-term knowledge.
Much of that consolidation appears to happen when our brains are offline. As we sleep, and during quiet rest , the hippocampus replays our recent experiences. This is thought to gradually distill those experiences and integrate them into the neocortex—the part of our brains that stores most of what we think of as knowledge.
Agent memory can use a similar division of labor. Agents capture much of their work in logs or transcripts. Researchers at Letta and UC Berkeley proposed sleep-time compute as a way for models to use idle time between interactions to reorganize their existing context. The same idea can help agents organize their memory by reflecting on logs to fix mistakes or produce new notes and representations. This process is often called dreaming (Figure 1).
We’ve found that dreaming has been a useful tool for helping us give Claude effective memory. In this post, we share how we’ve come to think about agent memory and walk through several evaluations we’ve used to explore agent memory, including the use of dreaming, and what each component contributes to memory organization.
Claude can use dreaming to organize memory. This can correct mistakes, create notes, build new memory representations, or shape what’s preemptively loaded into future sessions.
Memory notes
By “agent memory,” we mean knowledge that Claude gains from experience—including interactions with users and tasks it’s been assigned—and that it retains between sessions, saved as context it can read later. It excludes other ways models can learn or manage context, such as changes to their weights (the internal parameters set during training), in-context learning (knowledge gained within a single conversation), and compaction (summaries written by Claude that replace its older turns so it can continue working in a new context window).
In the human brain, chemical signals released before, during, or after an experience can mark a memory as important. Marked memories tend to be replayed more often than unmarked ones during offline periods. This process, called replay , helps stabilize and integrate them into long-term memory.
Similarly, Claude can tag salient events in a session log as they happen, so they’re easier to find later, or it can write them to a memory store, such as a folder of memory notes (Figure 2). But how can Claude tell what’s salient in the moment, before it knows what’s coming next?
Claude can write notes to memory.
Memory can be a prediction about what the future will need
Memory is, occasionally, a prediction. By writing down a rule, an agent predicts that the pattern it’s describing will be relevant again. For instance, writing down a verified fact is a prediction that an agent in a future session will want to rely on that fact without double-checking it. Over time, Claude has become much better at making these kinds of predictions.
Consider a task from Continual Learning Bench (CL-Bench) 1.0 , a benchmark that measures an agent’s ability to use memory in order to tackle long-horizon tasks. One particular task asks Claude to answer a series of questions by looking up information in a database. After Claude gives an answer, it’s told the correct solution and can write a memory to help answer future questions.
Memory can support a learning loop here. If Claude gets a question wrong, it can record the failure, come up with theories about what went wrong, test those theories, and turn what it finds into a rule about how to answer in the future.
We ran the CL-Bench 1.0 task using Claude Managed Agents . Claude started each question in a fresh session, with one exception: it could retrieve files from a memory directory that persisted from one session to the next.
Different models achieved different levels of success at creating their own learning loops. Claude Sonnet 4.6 got as far as generating theories about why an answer was wrong. Its memory directory contained a scattering of files, each listing several untested guesses.
CL-Bench database task, comparing memory with a stateless baseline across models.
Claude Opus 4.7 consolidated its notes into a single reference document and began marking which facts it had checked and which were still unconfirmed. Claude Sonnet 5 marked each answer as confirmed after the grader had checked it, and wrote a correction when it had answered wrong.
Claude Opus 5 was the first of these models to close the loop. Most of its entries included a rule (and also how it knew the rule was true), answers to earlier questions, and clear warnings about traps it had discovered along the way (Figure 3).
Like Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 both closed the loop, using memory to capture validated rules about how to best answer future questions. With memory, both scored about the same as Opus 5, though their baseline performance without memory was slightly higher.
Claude has learned to judge salience
We also evaluated Claude’s ability to play Pokémon Red , a game that challenges Claude to navigate complex long-horizon tasks, as a test of Claude’s judgment about what to save to memory. At the start of each run, we gave each model a folder of memory files that it could read from and write to while it played (Figure 4).
We compared the memory folders from one run each of Claude Sonnet 3.7 and Claude Fable 5, when each was about 10,000 steps into the game. A key difference we noticed was what each model thought was worth remembering. Sonnet 3.7 assumed everything might matter and wrote to memory indiscriminately. Its memory folder contained

8088 Domination Post-Mortem, Part 1
Posted by Trixter on June 19, 2014
These next few posts are a technical write-up of how I created 8088 Domination , which is a program that displays fairly decent full-motion video on a 1981 IBM PC. Before reading further, it might be worthwhile to familiarize yourself with the production itself if you haven’t seen it. Here is video of what it looks like running on a 1981 IBM PC 5150 connected to a TV via the composite output jack:
…and if you doubt the above video’s authenticity, you can download the production and run it on your own vintage hardware as proof.
I would like to apologize in advance for switching between past tense (ie. my thought process during the design phase) and present tense (when describing how to achieve certain objectives) throughout this write-up.
Background
I’ve been fascinated by desktop digital video for decades. Starting with the first Video For Windows tools in the early 1990s, using early capture hardware (like the Media Vision Pro Movie Spectrum , which captured directly into MSV1/CRAM format ), I’ve toyed with desktop video and its possibilities.
Of course, I’ve also been fascinated with demos since the early 1990s, and when you love two things that much, you find ways to mash them together. Many of my demoscene productions have had video as a part or whole of them in some way. Grind (1993) was a modplayer that displayed dancing Spring Break girls in perfect time to the music; the end-part of Explicit (1996) has dancing clubbers embedded in cubes, also dancing in perfect time to the music; and of course 8088 Corruption (2004) which displayed FMV on a 1981 IBM PC and took a chunk out of my 15 minutes .
8088 Corruption was not recognized for amazing quality video, but rather its novel solution to the problem of trying to display FMV on such a limited platform. That solution was to use 40×25 text mode , since that was the only mode represented in an amount of video memory that could be completely changed every frame without distracting artifacts or overtaxing the system.
I gave a talk in 2007 that explained 8088 Corruption in detail, and in that talk I explained that displaying FMV using CGA in graphics mode would be impossible. This is because CGA graphics mode uses 8x the amount of video memory that 8088 Corruption was handling. Even a simple calculation assuming 24fps video reveals that the amount of data needing to be updated per second (24fps * 16KB = 384KB/s) is outside of the IBM PC’s capability: CGA RAM can only be changed at a rate of 240KB/s, and most hard drives of the era operate at roughly 90KB/s. It sure felt impossible, so that’s why I said it.
Then I thought about the problem for 7 years.
Adjusting Expectations
I came to several realizations over the past few years thinking about this “impossible” problem. The most basic realization is that it isn’t always necessary to change every single pixel on the screen to show convincing FM

Firecracker VM Escape: PwnEscape Part 2
hn.text:
Firecracker is supposed to keep untrusted code inside a microVM. We escaped it and achieved code execution as root on the host.
We found how it saved registers, changed where it would resume, and made it execute a call of our choosing when it returned from KVM. The guest then restored the temporary stack changes. Firecracker kept running, and the VM remained accessible over SSH.
PwnEscape Part 1 introduced the host memory primitive behind this work. Here we follow the next part of the chain: using that access to find Firecracker in memory and take over a live thread from inside the guest. This is a continuation to show CVE-2026-99999 on a Firecracker setup.
00 / Choosing where to take control
A Firecracker microVM has a process on the host that manages it. Each virtual CPU, or vCPU, has a thread in that process. The thread enters KVM to run the guest and returns to Firecracker when an event needs handling in userspace. Firecracker documents this arrangement in its architecture overview .
firecracker-host-integration-dbdde36ef234
The call that runs the virtual CPU looks like this:
ioctl(vcpu_fd, KVM_RUN, 0 );
While the thread is in that system call, the host kernel holds its saved userspace registers in a structure called pt_regs . These registers describe the Firecracker thread: its instruction pointer says where execution should resume, and its stack pointer says which userspace stack it should use.
That made the return from KVM_RUN an attractive target. If we could locate and modify the saved frame, we could choose the code Firecracker executed when the thread returned to userspace. A guest operation that caused such a return would provide the trigger.
We already had access to selected host physical memory through a guest mapping. To use it, we needed to identify the Firecracker process, find code we could call in that process, and locate the register frame belonging to its active vCPU thread. The starting point was a page of memory we controlled inside the guest.
01-guest-to-vmm-chain-5c0fbee0cb07
Figure 1. The guest identifies its Firecracker process, finds the saved registers for a vCPU thread, and redirects the thread when it returns from KVM.
01 / Finding our guest page on the host
The guest and host use different physical address spaces. A page has a guest physical address, or GPA, inside the VM and a host physical address, or HPA, in the machine backing it. On the target, Extended Page Tables (EPT) provide the translation between them.
We placed a recognizable byte pattern, a nonce, in a guest page. The first resolver took that page's known GPA and its contents as inputs. Together, they gave us an address to translate and a way to check whether the translation reached our page.
The resolver searched the host physical ranges covered by the memory primitive for candidate EPT roots. An EPT root is the starting point of the translation tables. For each candidate, the resolver followed the entries selected by the guest address until it reached a physical page, then checked that page for the nonce.
The snippets below are explanatory pseudocode with descriptive helper names. They show the data passed between stages and the checks used to connect them.
for root in candidate_ept_roots:
page_hpa = walk_ept(root, guest_gpa)
if page_hpa is invalid:
continue
contents = read_host(page_hpa, length(nonce))
if contents == nonce:
candidates.append((root, page_hpa))
The nonce check connected a proposed translation to memory we controlled. The broader search produced two candidates; validation of the nested page tables reduced them to one EPT root. Walking that root gave us the host physical address of our guest page.
We called this result guest_page_hpa and passed it to the next resolver. We now had a recognizable object in host memory. The next task was finding the host process that mapped it.
02 / Finding the Firecracker process
Firecracker maps memory used by the guest into its own address space. That mapping gave us a way to work backward from the guest page to the process.
Host processes use page tables to translate their virtual addresses into physical memory. The top level is called the page global directory, or PGD. Recovering the appropriate PGD would let us translate addresses inside Firecracker and read its code and stack through the memory primitive.
Our reverse mapper searched the native host page tables for a mapping of guest_page_hpa . A normal page table walk starts with a virtual address and produces a physical address. Here, we looked for a mapping to a physical page we already knew, then recovered the virtual address and page table root associated with it.
The check runs in both directions:
for mapping in reverse_map_host_page_tables(guest_page_hpa):
pgd = mapping.root
guest_page_va = mapping.virtual_address
resolved_hpa = walk_host_page_tables(pgd, guest_page_va)
if resolved_hpa != guest_page_hpa:
continue
if read_host(resolved_hpa, length(nonce)) != nonce:
continue
process_candidates.append((pgd, guest_page_va))
This connected the host process's virtual mapping to the physical page found through EPT. The reverse mapper returned one validated address space. We retained its root as host_pgd and used it to inspect the process.
The next resolver looked for the Firecracker executable in those mappings. It identified an ELF image and checked a known byte sequence in Firecracker's write(2) wrapper. That connected the recovered address space to the binary we were targeting.
ASLR changes where an executable is loaded. The difference between an address in the ELF image and its corresponding runtime address is the load bias. Once the mapper had identified the image, it could recover that bias and use it to locate the code required by the exploit:
runtime_code_address = load_bias + code_address_in_elf
The mapper returned the load bias as firecracker_base . With that value and host_pgd , we could locate code in the running process, translate its virtual address to host physical memory, and

hn.title: Notes on San Marino
hn.text:
I spent three days in San Marino, a landlocked microstate completely surrounded by Italy. The people of San Marino are called the “Sammarinese.”
Travelling in Afghanistan is hard, but writing about Afghanistan is easy . If you are a white person in a place like Afghanistan, interesting things will happen to you. You don’t even have to do anything. Just stand on a street corner and strangers will stare at you and walk up to you and introduce themselves and shake your hand and offer you tea and food and show you around the city and you’ll find that it is harder to avoid getting into writing-worthy traveler adventures than to find them.
The European microstates of San Marino, Liechtenstein, Monaco, and Andorra have the opposite dynamic from a travel perspective. They are beautiful, wealthy, safe, lovely countries squarely rooted in one of the most beautiful, wealthy, safe, and lovely regions in the world. Hence, they are some of the most pleasantly boring/boringly pleasant countries in the world. Their populations are content, their governments are highly functional, their economies hum along, and nothing of note has happened in any of them since World War II.
So in a sense, travelling through these European microstates is the ultimate challenge of this blog. Not in the sense of paying that AK-wielding border guard $200 to let me out of Guinea was challenging, but in the sense that I needed to enhance my travel-writing focus to maximally mine pleasant dullness for anything interesting to write about.
I spent three days in San Marino, Liechtenstein, Monaco, and Andorra each , which, considering that they vary in geographic size from an American metro area to a large municipal park, and vary in population size from Bend, Oregon to Watertown, South Dakota, is a lot of time for each. I truly wanted to suck the travel marrow from these countries.
I’m not sure that I entirely succeeded and I’m not sure I’ll write about all of them, but first up is San Marino.
(Note – all images in this post can be expanded by clicking on them.)
Overview:
Population (2026) – 33,500 (5 th lowest in the world)
Population Growth Rate (2025) – 0%
Size – 23.6 square miles/61.2 square kilometers (a little bigger than Manhattan)
GDP (nominal, 2025) – $2.25 billion (less than the estimated net worth of Mr. Beast )
GDP growth rate (2025) – 1.5%
GDP per capita nominal (2025) – $65,543 (comparable to Austria or Kentucky)
GDP per capita PPP (2023) – $78,000 (compare to about $59,000 for Italy, or $55-60K for the two adjacent Italian provinces)
Inflation rate (2021-2024) – 1.24-5.93% (Euro)
Biggest export – “Washing and Bottling Machines”
Median age (2025) – 48.6 years
Life expectancy (2025) – 86 years (ranked #2 in the world on some lists )
Murder rate (2025) – 0 per 100,000
Ethnicity – I don’t think there are any official records, but presumably mostly Sammarinese and Italian
Religion (2023) – 85-95% Catholic
Olympic Medals – 3 (1 silver, 2 bronze, all from the 2020 Tokyo Olympics)
Geography
Normally I don’t describe national geographic layouts in these posts, but I think it’s worth doing for the European Microstates to emphasize their tininess and respective geopolitical oddities.
San Marino is situated in a hilly/mountainous region in northern-central Italy, wedged between two Italian provinces (Rimini and Pesaro e Urbino). The nearest significant population center is Rimini (~150,000 inhabitants), a somewhat rundown coastal beach city with typically beautiful Italian old towns and cathedrals. It took two trains over five hours for me to get from Rome to Rimini, from which almost everyone enters San Marino.
The Rimini-San Marino bus runs every hour from morning to night, is surprisingly convenient, and takes about 45 minutes to drop off passengers in the heart of San Marino. Like every other European Microstate (except Andorra), there are no border checkpoints around San Marino.
While waiting for the bus at 10 AM on a Wednesday, two ambiguously accented European men approached me, one of whom was shirtless. I soon learned that they were Bulgarian BMW salesmen on holiday in Italy, and they decided to take a boozy day trip to San Marino. I never learned why the one guy was shirtless, including throughout the entire bus ride, but I guess Bulgarians are going to Bulgarian.
The capital of the nation of San Marino is the City of San Marino, which is situated in the center of the country. The City of San Marino is one of nine castelli (Italian for “castle”), their term for municipalities, or perhaps more accurately in this case, tiny provinces. Castello populations range from 11,200 to 1,000, and the capital is actually only the third-largest at a little over 4,000 inhabitants, largely due to the City of San Marino being given almost entirely over to tourist and government functions (in that order).
Having done almost no research on San Marino before arriving, my first surprise was how rural the country feels. I guess I implicitly assumed that microstates tend to be compact and urban, like Vatican City or Monaco, but most of San Marino feels vast and empty. It’s a land of fairly steep rolling hills with nearly all stores and homes built along primary avenues with few side roads.
Serravalle, the largest castello (holding about one-third of the population), is the relative exception and is the most urban part of the country, at least in a modern sense. It is based on the northern border closest to Rimini, so the San Marino Mall and accompanying wholesalers claim most of the commercial traffic coming from Italy. Many Sammarinese live in Serravalle to make daily commutes for work in Rimini:
Serravalle also has a bunch of middle-class European residential neighborhoods:
Now that I’m looking at these pictures afterward, I’m noticing a bit of a beige-yellow-light brown color scheme…
Once the bus from Rimini gets through Serravalle, tourists find themselves in remote European hill country…
Peppered with small Sammarinese towns…

by Emma Roth
Nov 6, 2026, 3:00 PM UTC
Image: The Verge
Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.
Fox has officially closed its $22 billion acquisition of Roku, the companies announced on Friday . With Roku under its umbrella, Fox now controls a major streaming platform that reaches more than 100 million households in the US .
First announced in June , the deal will allow Fox to bring Fox Sports, news content, and local stations to Roku. “I would expect that we can grow our viewership in the US with a combination of Roku technology, Roku’s platform, the tremendous content that’s on The Roku Channel, and the content that Fox brings to it as well,” Fox CEO Lachlan Murdoch said at the time. Along with Roku, Fox also operates its own Fox One streaming service and the free streamer Tubi.
Related
Fox wants to take over your TV — and the tech inside it
Pour one out for Roku City
Though the deal might change what Roku showcases on its platform, it doesn’t look like it will affect the open nature of Roku’s streaming ecosystem. The Department of Justice says Fox has committed to keeping Roku “an open and neutral content partner post-merger.” That includes allowing Roku to carry non-Fox content for at least three years and not discriminating against rival content in search results. It also committed to continuing to allow users to rearrange the apps and tiles on Roku’s home screen.
“We started Roku more than two decades ago to give people a better way to watch TV, and that mission doesn’t change today. What does change is our reach and resources,” Roku founder Anthony Wood said. “Fox has a deep respect for Roku’s culture and wholly shares our commitment to staying open to every content partner.” Wood now serves on Fox’s board of directors.
Update, November 6th: Added information from the DOJ.

Fast and cost-effective at scale
Beyond the lower price, the workflow keeps costs down: you can draft fast at 360p or 720p, fix a detail with a follow-up edit instead of re-generating the entire clip, and then upscale your best creations to 1080p or 4K.
Longer clips up to 15 seconds
You can now generate and edit videos natively up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 seconds with Omni 1.1. You can also specify duration in one-second increments from 3 to 15 seconds, giving you room to tell complete stories, create product explainers, or produce full social ad spots in a single generation.

You can refine the same clip turn by turn — such as swapping a product or background, changing the lighting or weather, or switching the aspect ratio — instead of starting over from scratch. Tesla to wind down production of Cybertruck
01:31

Share

Nov. 6, 2026, 8:36 AM EST / Source : Reuters
By Reuters
Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around mid-2027, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday, after years of persistently weak sales for a futuristic model once touted as a rival to legacy pickup trucks that ultimately only sold in just a handful of markets because of its heavy, angular design.
Musk said in an X post the production wind-down would enable the automaker to accommodate increased output of its newly launched Cybercab model, which the billionaire has made central to Tesla's robotaxi ambitions.
While it was not immediately clear whether Cybertruck production would be moved to another facility or phased out entirely, the automaker's Austin plant is the only known Tesla facility equipped to manufacture the model's specialized components.
In response to a user on X, Musk called the Cybertruck the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made" and the wind-down the "end of an era."
Tesla did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment sent outside regular business hours.
The US EV maker only began delivering the Cybertruck to customers in late 2023. According to Kelley Blue Book, the company only sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down 48% from 38,965 in 2024. Before the pickup truck launched, Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 units.
"It doesn't make sense to keep it going when it's not meeting its targets," said former Aston Martin CEO Andy Palmer. "Every rational auto guy would say the same."
"It will no doubt only be a rounding error on Tesla's balance sheet, but the statistics speak for themselves."
Right from its unveiling in 2019, the Cybertruck was a controversial choice for Musk. Its angular design was mocked by pickup truck purists and safety experts predicted it would be hard to gain approval for sale in key markets like Europe.
The unveiling event itself was marred when Musk tried to prove that its windows were shatterproof by having metal balls thrown at them - only to leave massive cracks in two of them.
During Cybertruck's official launch in 2023, Musk touted it as a futuristic competitor to pickup trucks from General Motors and Ford, saying "finally, the future will look like the future."
But the vehicle has struggled to meet those expectations.
Automotive analyst Automotive analyst Felipe Munoz said that although the Cybertruck has been called a failure because of its poor sales, electric pick-ups from Ford and others have also flopped in the US market.
"All of them lost the competition because electric pick ups aren't popular in the US," Munoz said.
But Cybertruck's sharp-edged stainless-steel design limited its prospects in markets like Europe where EVs are more popular. Regulatory approval was impossible for Europe because of rules there concerning pedestrian impact.
"Anywhere where you have crash regulation that takes into account pedestrian impact, that Cybertruck won't go, can't go," former Aston Martin CEO Palmer said.
The Cybercab, which has butterfly doors and no steering wheel, pedals or mirrors, is one of Musk's key bets in his push to turn Tesla into an AI and robotics company rather than just an automaker.
Musk has said he sees it as Tesla's main autonomous model supplying a global network of robotaxis.
After years of delays to Musk's self-driving targets, Tesla began offering paid rides in a small fleet of Cybercabs in Austin in September. However, the automaker still has to answer the US auto safety agency's questions on whether it has properly self-certified Cybercab to demonstrate compliance with federal motor vehicle safety standards.
"Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab," Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X.

hn.title: Can GROUP BY still be optimized after all these years?
hn.text:
← All posts
One of the things I like the most about the world of databases is how a simple operation can become extremely complex when it's optimized to its highest levels.
As part of that line of thought - I thought it might be interesting and fun to share a novel optimization we recently found that improved Pivot's performance significantly on GROUP BY queries that find the top K groups by aggregate value. For example, "which 10 items have the most orders?":
SELECT item_id, COUNT (*) AS c
FROM orders
GROUP BY item_id
ORDER BY c DESC
LIMIT 10 ;
How do "regular" GROUP BYs run on analytical databases?
Although every database wants to think it's unique - most of them (Pivot included ;)) performs GROUP BY in a very similar way when the grouping keys have high cardinality (IE there are many groups in the GROUP BY).
First, each CPU thread in the database receives a slice of the input data to read from disk, decode, and prepare for aggregation:
Each thread then divides its decoded data into X partitions based on the grouping key and aggregates each partition separately. For example, ClickHouse uses 256 partitions, so each thread maintains its own set of 256 hash tables, one per partition:
* Pivot uses a different method here instead of a hash table, but that’s a story for another blog post ;)
Keeping these hash tables private to each thread lets the threads aggregate the data independently, without acquiring locks or writing to the same memory locations, which would cause contention between CPU caches.
Once all threads finish this initial aggregation, each worker is assigned a range of partitions to merge. For each partition, the worker gathers the partial aggregates produced by all threads and combines them into the final aggregates for that partition’s groups:
Once every partition has been merged, the database produces the complete GROUP BY result by concatenating the results from all partitions:
Is all this work actually needed?
While this process definitely outputs a correct result, in some (very common) query patterns, this GROUP BY algorithm performs much more work than is actually needed. Specifically, in queries where not all the aggregation results are used in the final answer - many of the groups and partitions are aggregated when they don't actually need to.
Take our earlier example: “Which 10 items have the most orders?”
SELECT item_id, COUNT (*) AS c
FROM orders
GROUP BY item_id
ORDER BY c DESC
LIMIT 10 ;
If our system uses 4,096 partitions, the top 10 items can belong to at most 10 of them. That leaves at least 4,086 partitions whose results contribute nothing to the final answer—yet we still spend a-lot of time and compute merging them.
Queries in this pattern are pretty common in workloads we see: “Which 100 items in our warehouse have the highest review scores?”, “Who are our 50 biggest paying customers?”, “Which posts on our platform received the most likes in the last 24 hours?”. Given that, we thought it was worth exploring whether these queries could be optimized!
So how can we avoid all this work?
To solve this redundant work issue, we looked for a structure that could help us prune some of the partitions as we progress through the aggregation phase. As big lovers of Bloom filters (and the proud owners of i-love-bloom-filters.com !), we thought a probabilistic, hash-based structure might help us achieve this goal.
The most "naive" implementation we could think about was to simply maintain a global counter or aggregate for each partition and use it later to decide which partitions to skip.
For our “items with the most orders” query, that means keeping a counter of the total number of orders in each partition:
During the merge stage, before merging each new partition, we can compare its total order count against the smallest count in our current TopK results.
If the partition’s total is smaller, we can safely skip merging it entirely: no individual group can have more orders than the partition as a whole, so none of its groups can affect our current TopK result.
If the partition’s total is larger, though, we still need to merge it, do the heavy CPU work, and find out whether any of its groups is actually large enough to affect our TopK result.
While this approach is pretty cool and can help prune partitions in some scenarios, it requires a pretty extreme distribution of aggregate values across groups.
To prune a partition, the average aggregate value across its groups must be orders of magnitude smaller than the smallest value in our current TopK.
For example, suppose the top 10 order counts we’ve calculated so far range from 1,000 to 1,300. If a partition contains 100 items with exactly 15 orders each, our pruning logic can’t skip it: the partition’s total is 1,500 orders, which exceeds our smallest TopK value - even though none of its individual groups comes close.
Because our pruning logic only considers the total number of orders in each partition, it can’t distinguish between two cases: 100 items with 15 orders each, which we could safely prune, and 99 items with one order each plus one item with 1,401 orders, which we must merge because that item belongs in our TopK. Both partitions contain 1,500 orders, but only the second contains an item that would change the result.
To overcome this, we looked for a method that builds on the same idea but gives us more control over the granularity of pruning.
The method we came up with was to give each partition a fixed number of “slots.” Each group maps to one slot, and that slot tracks the combined order count of all groups mapped to it. Since no group’s count can exceed its slot’s total, we can safely prune a partition if every slot’s total is below the smallest value in our current TopK .
For example, suppose again our current top order counts range from 1,000 to 1,300. A partition containing 100 items with 15 orders each has a total of 1,500, so the partition-level counter alone won’t let us prune it. But if those items are s

hn.title: The planet Vulcan: a cautionary tale
hn.text:
The planet Vulcan: a cautionary tale that deserves to be better known
The planet Vulcan was first allegedly sighted in 1859, having been proposed
to orbit the Sun inside the orbit of Mercury. Further sightings were
made over the next forty years or so. The properties of Vulcan
were described in detail, despite the fact that astronomers are now
firmly convinced that it does not exist. What actually was
sighted and attributed to Vulcan remains an open question.
That scientists were confident of something that later turned out to
be incorrect is hardly breaking news. After all, the inherent vulnerability
of scientific theories to falsification is largely what gives the
scientific method its credibility.
However, the story of Vulcan is an cautionary one, providing a number of
lessons that contemporary scientists and science
students would do well learn.
Incidentally, this article is not about Mr Spock's home-world. Presumably,
the choice of the name Vulcan for this other fictional planet is
a coincidence. But it would nice to think it was intentional.
The birth of Vulcan
Our story starts in 1821, when French astronomer Alexis Bouvard published
detailed observations of the orbital behaviour of the planet Uranus, which
had been discovered about fifty years previously. Almost immediately,
astronomers who examined Bouvard's work realised that the
orbit of Uranus was not entirely in agreement with predictions made
by Newton's laws of motion and universal gravitation. These laws were
were already solidly established, and considered to be more-or-less
unchallengeable at the time.
Over the next twenty years or so, Bouvard and other astronomers came to
appreciate that
the anomalous orbit of Uranus could be explained if there were another,
as-yet unidentified planetary body exerting a gravitational influence on it.
Predicting the orbital path of such a body -- if, indeed, it even existed --
was a mathematical, rather than an astronomical, problem --
and an extremely difficult one.
French mathematician Urbain Le Verrier is generally credited with
performing the calculations that allowed the new planet, now known
as Neptune, to be indentified. It was definitively observed in 1846,
within one degree of the location that Le Verrier had predicted.
This was, and remains, a strikingly successful application of Newton's
mathematics to the modelling of planetary motion.
Whilst working on the mathematics of the orbit of Uranus, Le Verrier
also began studying the orbit of Mercury. He published a detailed
theory of the behaviour of Mercury, again based on Newton's laws,
in 1859. His results were a very close match to the observed
behaviour of the planet but, as had been the case for Uranus earlier,
not a perfect one. In particular, the precession of Mercury's
perihelion -- the variation in the point at which Mercury comes
closest to the Sun --
was larger than predicted, by the vanishingly-small amount of
43 arc-seconds per century. That's about one ten-thousandth part of
a degree per year.
Given the success of Le Verrier's theoretical work leading to the discovery
of Neptune, it's entirely understandable that he proposed a similar mechanism
to explain the behaviour of Mercury. Le Verrier gave the name Vulcan
to this putative planet, and astronomers immediately began looking
for it.
The rise of Vulcan
Vulcan was "discovered" almost immediately. Le Verrier was officially
recognized as the discoverer in 1860, although he did not make the
confirmatory observations. The clincher -- or so it must have seemed to
Le Verrier -- was an observation of Vulcan's transit of the Sun (that
is, the passage of the planet across the sun's disc).
However, even Le Verrier must have realized that this observation
had been made in non-ideal conditions: a smallish telescope and
crude timekeeping equipment.
Still, over the next forty
years many sightings of Vulcan were published, some by reputable
astronomers working with state-of-the-art equipment. In particular,
respected US astronomers
James Craig Watson and Lewis Swift -- already credited with the
discoveries of numerous
astronomical bodies -- both reported sightings of
Vulcan in 1878. Both men reported that Vulcan was red in colour, and appeared
as a definite disc. This last point is highly significant because,
in principle, it rules out the mistaken observation of a star. Even in state-of-the-art modern telescopes, a star usually appears only as a point of light;
only bodies within our solar system are close enough appear as a disc.
In the end, at least twenty sightings of Vulcan were published by at
least ten astronomers with some standing. It seems probable that a huge
number of less reliable sightings were made as well. The consensus
in the astronomical community at the end of the nineteenth century
was almost certainly that Vulcan
existed, even if was observed only fleetingly.
The fall of Vulcan
It has to be admitted that the existence of Vulcan was somewhat contentious
right from the start. French astronomer Emmanuel Liais asserted that
he had been observing the Sun at the same time as Le Verrier's initial
reported transit, and with better equipment -- and he'd seen nothing.
There's little doubt that some of the alleged transits were, in fact,
sunspots; and some of the reported bright objects just stars.
Moreover, the various reported sightings did not always confirm
Le Verrier's mathematical model perfectly. He continued to adjust the parameters
of the model to accommodate all the sightings, but the agreement
with observation was never strikingly good. Nevertheless, Le Verrier
was able to publish detailed values for the radius of Vulcan's orbit
(about thirteen million miles),
its period of revolution (about 20 days), and a number of other
orbital properties.
It's probably fair to say that nobody now believes that there is
a planet with the properties that Le Verrier predicted, although
the existence of some planet within the orbit of Mercury
can't be ruled out. In fact, the I

hn.title: America's economy is becoming zero-sum
hn.text:
Economics
Add Topic
American capitalism was a win-win. We've abandoned it to bet | Opinion
If all of this money went into the capital markets instead, it would finance the growth of companies through innovation and entrepreneurship, as well as infrastructure that girds the economy.
Daniel Altman
Opinion contributor
Nov. 7, 2026, 6:02 a.m. ET
Hear this story
The genius of economics is that it’s filled with win-win situations. Every time a buyer and seller agree to a transaction, they should both be made better off.
For most of our history, this is also how Americans got rich. But now, rather than making the pie bigger, Americans are more focused on taking someone else’s slice.
We can see it in how young people are using their money.
Gen Z, millennials keep their money in prediction markets. That's a problem
More than a quarter of Gen Z and millennials surveyed together by Global Strategy Group said they participated in prediction markets, versus 10% of Gen X and just 2% of baby boomers.
About 40% of Americans ages 18-49 told the Siena Research Institute that they had a sports betting account, compared with 16% of those 50 to 64 and 4% of those 65 and older.
And cryptocurrency holdings among the younger generations are more than twice as prevalent as among the older, according to JPMorganChase.
Unlike stocks and bonds, all of these so-called investments are zero-sum .
For someone to win in a prediction market or sports bet, someone else has to lose. There’s no increase in the economy’s productive capacity . The same goes for cryptocurrencies, most of which have value based solely on supply and demand rather than any intrinsic usefulness. People who hold cryptocurrency only see their wealth increase when more people want to hold it. And this is where the younger generations are keeping their money.
If all of this money went into the capital markets instead, it would finance the growth of companies and spending by governments. Some of it might be wasted on perks and pointless programs, but most of it would fund innovation and entrepreneurship, as well as the infrastructure that girds the economy.
These are the true engines of higher living standards , yet money is being sucked away from them by zero-sum gambles.
Zero-sum game is a drag on US economic growth
These trends among individuals parallel recent moves in government and the corporate sector.
Washington has been trying to limit trade with tariffs , destroying more win-win possibilities for American companies and consumers. The Trump administration has also threatened other countries to take control of their resources: oil in Venezuela , critical minerals in Greenland and whatever the endgame might be in Iran .
Meanwhile, the families of the people in power have enriched themselves through connections and privilege rather than economic ingenuity.
In the corporate sector, businesses ranging from big-box stores to coffee shops have delved deeper into the world of personalized pricing, using data on consumers to set prices as close as possible to the most they would pay.
When consumers can only buy goods and services at their maximum price, then each transaction is no longer a win-win. Only the seller gains any extra benefit beyond their costs; consumers never feel like they got a bargain.
Investing corporate resources in this zero-sum money grab rather than new or better products creates a drag on economic growth, too. Growth is where the rubber meets the road in our economy, and not just for living standards.
Without strong growth in the nation’s incomes – and the resulting tax revenue – our enormous national debt will become even more difficult to sustain. We run the risk of a collapse in our currency, our wealth and our way of life if we continue to engage in zero-sum thinking.
It’s time to return to the more productive forms of capitalism that built our prosperity in the first place.
Daniel Altman is the author of “ The Best Decisions You’ll Ever Make: An Economist’s Guide to Saving Time, Making Money, and Living Well ” and the " High Yield Economics " newsletter.

hn.title: Devvm.dev: One VM for every project
hn.text:
Free and open source One VM for every project
An isolated sandbox with your project’s toolchain, ready for you or a coding agent to start coding.
Install
Read the docs
Quick start
macOS Linux
# Install devvm, and Lima with it
brew trust --formula devvmhq/tap/devvm
brew install devvmhq/tap/devvm
The install script in the Linux tab also works on macOS, and Installing lists its options.
# Install devvm and what it needs
curl -fsSL https://github.com/devvmhq/devvm/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash
The script asks before it installs Lima, QEMU or access to /dev/kvm .
1. Go to your project
Open a terminal and cd into any project folder.
2. Run devvm
devvm shows what the new VM gets. Confirm to make it, or customize it.
3. Start your agent
devvm opens a shell in the VM, whose prompt starts with (devvm) , so start your agent there.
Claude Code needs your Claude login before its first start, which devvm agent login claude makes from the VM and keeps on your machine ( your first VM ). The next time you run devvm in the folder, it opens the same VM, and devvm tools adds an agent to a VM you already have.
What’s supported
Toolchains
devvm chooses the toolchains your project’s files call for, and you can choose more when you customize a new VM or name them with --tools ( toolchains ).
Coding agents
Claude Code, Codex and opencode run in the VM. Choose one when you customize a new VM, or choose them for every new VM in devvm setup ( coding agents ).
Layers
devvm ships the docker , nix and desktop layers, which you choose when you customize a new VM, and devvm layer new creates your own custom layers you can apply to any of your VMs ( layers ).
Why use devvm?
Developers face attacks every day, such as supply chain attacks , leaked secrets, prompt injections and rogue agents.
A sandbox limits the blast radius of an attack to what’s inside it.
You know you should run your code and agents in a sandbox, but most tools need configuration and setup that’s hard to get right.
devvm ships with sensible defaults so you can start coding in a sandbox with a single command.
Developer ready, zero config
The base image comes with optional extras that you choose, such as oh-my-bash, fzf, zoxide ( z ), tree and tldr.
Every VM gets your git name and email, so the commits made in it are authored by you or your agent.
Ports forward on their own, so a dev server on :5173 in the VM opens at localhost:5173 on your machine ( ports ).
devvm code opens the VM in VS Code over Remote-SSH ( devvm code ).
Isolated sandbox
The VM mounts your project folder at the same path. Apart from your agents’ settings from devvm’s own store, which it gets read-only, it sees nothing else in your home folder ( what a VM can reach ).
New VMs get the allowlist network tier by default, so they reach only an allowlist of hosts, through a proxy on your machine. You can choose a looser tier, internet or open, or a stricter one, none.
On macOS, devvm locks .git ’s hooks and config, so the VM can’t change what git runs on your machine ( .git protection ).
With --clone , the VM works on a clone of the repo of its own instead of your folder, so nothing in it can touch your working tree or .git , and its work reaches your repo only when you fetch it.
No sandbox closes every gap, so attack vectors lists what’s left open, and staying safe lists the habits that close most of it.
Ready in seconds
The first VM builds a base image, and every later VM is a copy of it that starts in seconds ( images ).
devvm builds each version of a toolchain once and shares it read-only, so all VMs use the same copy ( shared tools ).
Made for coding agents
The agent runs in the VM, so an attack on it stays in the sandbox. It gets your settings, skills and MCP servers but never your history ( coding agents ).
On every network tier, their secrets, such as your Claude Code token and your Codex login, stay on your machine, because the VM gets placeholders and devvm’s proxy puts the real ones into its requests on the way out.
Make it yours
Your own layers are setup scripts that devvm builds into an image: devvm layer new mailpit starts one, and devvm --layers mailpit makes a VM with it ( your own layers ).
devvm setup --layers gives every new VM the layers you choose, so your shell setup, aliases or dotfiles can go in a layer of your own that each VM gets unless you leave it out ( extras of your own ).
--from starts the base image from a container image instead of Ubuntu’s, such as node:24 or your team’s own ( starting from a container image ).
When the project has a devcontainer.json , devvm sets up its VM from the file’s container image, ports, environment and commands ( devcontainer.json ).
FAQ
What does it run on?
devvm runs on macOS and on Linux, on arm64 or x86_64. It needs Lima , which runs the VMs with Apple’s Virtualization framework on macOS and QEMU on Linux ( backends ). Homebrew installs Lima along with devvm, and on Linux, Lima also needs QEMU and access to /dev/kvm . Installing lists every requirement, and known limits lists what Linux hosts lack, such as .git protection.
Does the agent run on my machine?
No. You start the agent in the VM’s shell, so it runs in the VM, and you never install it on your machine. There it sees only what the VM can reach .
Is it free?
Yes. devvm is open source under the MIT license .
Start coding in a sandbox
Install devvm , then run devvm in any project folder.
Install
Read the docs

Restaurant Delivery Payment-Skimming Campaign
hn.text:
← All news November 5, 2026
Scamwich: Inside a Restaurant Delivery Payment-Skimming Campaign
InfoHawk research has uncovered a network of 820 suspicious restaurant domains impersonating major US chains, including Jersey Mike's, Jimmy John's, Firehouse Subs, Chipotle, and Dave's Hot Chicken. Some are running sophisticated payment-skimming attacks that capture credit card information and ask customers for their bank's SMS verification codes.
Source: jarrysaymlckess[.]delivery and dawechlckhort[.]delivery
When customers order food online, they expect a familiar experience: find
their restaurant, choose their meal, and pay. Increasingly, criminals are
exploiting that familiarity by creating convincing clones of restaurant
ordering websites, right down to the original site's underlying code.
In early November 2026, InfoHawk researchers investigated a collection of
suspicious websites that appear to be part of one or more coordinated
restaurant impersonation and payment-skimming operations.
Across two research passes, we identified 820 domains impersonating 35
restaurant brands. Of those, 808 use the .delivery top-level
domain, and the rest use .com or .shop .
The scale is concerning, but what makes these sites particularly dangerous
is how convincing they can be.
These aren't ordinary fake websites
The investigation began with a suspicious domain:
mlckessejersstey[.]delivery .
The site impersonated Jersey Mike's, the popular sandwich chain, and
reproduced its online ordering experience.
Rather than simply displaying a crude imitation of the restaurant's website,
the attackers used a more sophisticated approach: reverse-proxying the
legitimate site while replacing the checkout payment form with a malicious
one.
A reverse proxy can retrieve content from a legitimate website and present
it to visitors under a different domain. This allows an attacker-controlled
site to display genuine pages and assets while selectively modifying the
parts of the experience that matter to the attacker.
In this case, the malicious checkout requested credit card information and
also asked customers for the SMS verification code sent by their bank.
This is a particularly dangerous combination. Capturing a credit card number
is valuable to criminals; obtaining a one-time verification code could also
help them authorize fraudulent transactions, depending on how the victim's
bank uses that code.
For consumers, the experience can appear nearly indistinguishable from
ordering directly from the restaurant. The site looks familiar, the menu and
ordering flow can behave normally, and the fraudulent payment form appears
at the moment a customer expects to pay.
Importantly, this does not require the legitimate restaurant's website to
have been hacked. The attackers can operate on infrastructure they control
while using the authentic restaurant website as the source of the content
they display.
Impersonated brands
Mostly .delivery typosquats, plus a few look-alike
.com and .shop names, found across two research
passes. "Seen" is the range of registration or scan dates we have for a
brand's domains, all in 2026. Open a brand to see its domains.

hn.title: Port 0: The Port That Does Not Exist
hn.text:
ACIDVEGAS
most dangerous motherfuck x come get some
The Port That Does Not Exist
2026-11-06
Port 0 is the port you are not supposed to use, so nobody looks there. So we put an IRC network on it. Then I got curious whether anyone else had, and scanned all of IPv4 for port 0. Turns out we weren't alone, and some of our neighbours really shouldn't be there.
Ask any program to listen on port 0 and it will hand you a socket on port 47193...or 58037...or whatever the kernel felt like that day. Port 0 is not a port you can have. It is the number you pass when you want the operating system to pick one for you.
But a TCP header is just bytes. The destination port field is 16 bits wide, and 0x0000 fits in 16 bits as well as anything else does. Nothing on the wire stops a packet from being addressed to port 0. Your tools will refuse it, your browser will block it, and your scanner's default port list skips it, because everyone agrees it isn't a real port.
Which makes it a pretty good place to hide things, whether anyone meant to or not. So we did some TCP cowboy shit & port scanned the entire fucking internet for open ports on port 0, which uncovered some interesting unexpected findings.
What Port 0 Actually Is
The standards are thin on this. RFC 9293 , the 2022 consolidation of the TCP spec, defines the source and destination port as "16 bits" and leaves it there. It has no rule against zero.
IANA lists 0/tcp and 0/udp as Reserved , pointing at RFC 6335 . That RFC splits the port space into System (0–1023), User (1024–49151) and Dynamic (49152–65535) ranges, and explains what "Reserved" means:
Reserved port numbers include values at the edges of each range, e.g., 0, 1023, 1024, etc., which may be used to extend these ranges or the overall port number space in the future.
So port 0 is not forbidden. It is set aside. The only place zero has a defined protocol meaning is UDP: RFC 768 makes the source port optional, and "if not used, a value of zero is inserted." TCP has nothing like that.
Why You Can't Listen On It
Port 0's reputation comes from the sockets API, not the wire. When you call bind() with sin_port = 0 , you are not asking for port 0. You are asking for any port. The ip(7) man page lists every case where Linux hands out an ephemeral port: bind() with port 0, listen() on an unbound socket, connect() on an unbound socket, and sendto() on an unbound datagram socket.
The range comes from net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range , which defaults to 32768 60999 on Linux, not the 49152–65535 that IANA calls Dynamic. And asking for port 0 needs no privileges. __inet_bind() only checks CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE when the requested port is non-zero.
How the kernel picks is more interesting than I expected. In net/ipv4/inet_connection_sock.c (v6.8), inet_csk_find_open_port() starts at a random offset and then does this:
offset = get_random_u32_below(remaining);
/* __inet_hash_connect() favors ports having @low parity
* We do the opposite to not pollute connect() users.
*/
offset |= 1U;
It walks the range in steps of two. The function above it says it outright: "We try to allocate an odd port (and leave even ports for connect())." Outgoing connections go through __inet_hash_connect() in inet_hashtables.c , which implements RFC 6056 Algorithm 4 (double-hash port selection) and takes the even ports first. The kernel splits the range by parity so servers asking for "any port" and clients making outbound connections don't fight over the same numbers. If SO_REUSEADDR is set, bind() also tries the lower half of the range before the upper half.
That is easy to test. On a stock Ubuntu box running Linux 6.8:
Test Result
2,000 × bind(("127.0.0.1", 0)) ports 32777–60997, 2,000 / 2,000 odd
same, with SO_REUSEADDR ports 32773–46835 (lower half only), all odd
listen() with no bind() port 58037
300 × connect() with no bind() source ports 32772–60998, 300 / 300 even
So when your program says "listen on port 0", the kernel hears "give me an odd number between 32768 and 61000." No normal program can listen on port 0.
So We Did It Anyways
You can bypass all of this with raw sockets, but if you just want to cheat, you can simply forward the port to another with iptables/nftables. As a fun proof of concept, I set up my IRC network at irc.supernets.org to accept plaintext connections on port 0 and SSL connections on port 1 . JUST TO FLEX. 😎
-A PREROUTING -p tcp -m tcp --dport 0 -j REDIRECT --to-ports 6667
-A PREROUTING -p tcp -m tcp --dport 1 -j REDIRECT --to-ports 6697
A SYN arrives for port 0, netfilter rewrites the destination to 6667 where the ircd is actually listening, and the reply is rewritten back on the way out. The ircd never knows. Port 1 does the same for TLS on 6697.
Talking To Port 0 Is Its Own Problem
Getting a server onto port 0 was the easy part. Getting a client there is where tools give up. I pointed everything I had at our own server on port 0:
Client Result
OpenBSD nc nc: port number too small: 0
telnet (inetutils) Port number 0 is out of range.
Chromium net::ERR_UNSAFE_PORT (port 1 too)
socat connects, works
Python asyncio connects, works
Python ssl on a blocking socket BlockingIOError
That last one is strange, because the TCP connection underneath it is fine. The problem is that the kernel says it isn't, and it does that on purpose. Here is inet_getname() in net/ipv4/af_inet.c , which backs getpeername() :
if (peer) {
if (!inet->inet_dport ||
(((1 << sk->sk_state) & (TCPF_CLOSE | TCPF_SYN_SENT)) &&
peer == 1)) {
release_sock(sk);
return -ENOTCONN;
}
Linux uses "destination port is 0" as its internal marker for "this socket isn't connected to anything." A socket that really is connected to port 0 trips that check, so getpeername() returns ENOTCONN on a working connection.
Python's ssl.wrap_socket() calls getpeername() to decide whether the socket is connected, gets ENOTCONN , decides it isn't, switches to non-blocking and tries a recv(1) , gets EAGAIN , and raises BlockingIOError . The TCP connection is fine. It just

hn.text:
Though voters in the US may not be excited to hear it , AMD's CEO is all in on data centers.
"We are a data center first company; that is our profile," Lisa Su said in an interview with Yahoo Finance . AMD's data center business was expected to grow by another 50% over the next three months, and AMD is looking to double that growth as it enters 2027, she said.
"We are extremely ambitious," Su added. "I want to be the best partner to the largest users of compute in the world," given that "AI and superintelligence [are] becoming more and more essential to every aspect of our lives and...business."
You May Also Like
Although tech stocks took a beating this week following the US elections, AMD, Nvidia, and their contemporaries are making record profits. While Nvidia is the world's most valuable company, AMD still made a record $13.4 billion in Q3 , almost 100% more than last year. A record 63% came from data centers.
"We are a tech company that has a lot of resources and the ability to expand our supply and expand our ability to help our customers and that's what's led to [this] tremendous growth," Su told Yahoo Finance.
None of this bodes well for consumer graphics cards, whose prices have exploded in recent months. Nvidia's RTX 5090 has all but disappeared from online retailers, with the 5080 going for far above MSRP . As for AMD, while its GPUs are still better value for the money than Nvidia's, its prices are no less encouraging and seem destined to follow Nvidia's to the moon.
Recommended by Our Editors
ASRock AMD Radeon RX 9070 GRE Steel Legend 12GB OC Review: A Midrange Standout in a Chaotic GPU Market
US Voters Reject AI Data Centers, Elon Musk Finds Solace in Orbital Alternative
Google's AI Mode Suddenly Can't Recall Who Won the 2020 Presidential Election
The flagship RX 9070 XT is over $900 right now. While that's $500 cheaper than its Nvidia equivalent, the RTX 5070 Ti, it's still $300 over its launch price. The RX 9070 non-XT is around $750, $200 over its MSRP. Entry-level cards like the RX 9060 XT with 16GB of VRAM are now over $700, too. Only the 8GB cards are remotely affordable, but even those are over $500.
It's clear from the pricing, if not Su's statements, where AMD and other tech firms are focusing their efforts. We'll have to see if voter backlash will slow down that momentum in the US. (Remember when Satya Nadella pitched Microsoft as "the Copilot company" in 2023?)

hn.title: Show HN: Waymark – A workflow engine that compiles jobs instead of replaying
hn.text: Hey everyone! @mozgiii and I have been working on Waymark for the better part of the last year. Waymark’s an open source durable execution library with similar functionality to Temporal or DBOS. I fell in love with durable execution a few years ago, after working at a company with a heavy pubsub architecture. In comparison to job orchestrators that force a certain task design or special syntax, many of these durable libs lets you write business logic in regular code: `asyncio.gather` to parallelize tasks, `for` loops, conditionals, and let the runtime figure out how to run them efficiently across a cluster of nodes. But most of the current solutions require a heavy broker, runtime hacks to try to ensure deterministic workflow logic, and feel like you have to learn a whole new ecosystem just to get started. A few unique design decisions in waymark: — Write jobs in normal code (right now Python but JS coming soon). Instead of running control flow as-is, which requires booting up an interpreter to replay past state, we’ll just compile your code directly. We walk your AST and map your logic to our stackless VM bytecode. We support variables, conditionals, await, sleep, helper functions, loops... basically what you’d expect in workflow logic. — Since we’re compiling a language subset, we can proactively flag errors in your workflows locally instead of when they run in production. — It only requires Postgres as the task broker. We’ve spent a lot of time tuning our design to play nicely with its strengths and limitations; our current benchmarks show around 1500 workflows/second but we still have some more optimization work to do here. — Actions plug-and-play with FastAPI’s dependency injection syntax. So if you already have an ecosystem based on typehinting/DI, it should fit like a glove. It allows for parallelization of workflows across one machine or a whole cluster. The bulk of the work per node is done by our central Rust core - which distributes workflows to properly saturate all cores. The idea is to be as batteries included as possible with the broker, webapp, and runtime. What to use it for? It works great as the runner loop controlling agents, but it also works well for basically any task that you need to kick off in the background. It’s largely replaced our way of writing api code. Most frontend actions at this point just push to a simple REST endpoint that kick off a background job. I spent an embarrassing amount of time making our https://waymark.sh site interactive - it’s probably the best place to learn more. We’re starting with Python support and looking for community input on what language to ship next. Would love to hear your thoughts!

hn.title: Blender's UI and Runtime: Much Faster Than GPUI
hn.text:
BUI
Blender's user interface, as a library you can use from Python, Rust, JavaScript (React, Svelte), C, C++ and Dear ImGui.
People spent decades building and optimizing Blender's GUI. It's battery and memory efficient, and super duper fast. We decoupled it, to give everyone a chance to build their own products with it. It supports multiple languages and frameworks, so you won't miss a beat!
Website and full documentation: bui.preetham.top · Chat: Discord
This README is a small book. Read it front to back for the whole story, or
jump to the chapter you need. Every chapter links to a longer guide in
docs/ or on the website when there's
more to say.

Part I: Welcome
1. What BUI is
BUI takes the user interface of Blender (its widget
drawing, its interaction rules and its look) and turns it into a standalone UI
library with a small C core. Your code builds the widget tree and handles
callbacks. Layout, input, drawing and presenting all happen in fast native code,
on the CPU or the GPU.
At the heart of BUI is the kit : a small runtime written in C. The kit
holds every widget in one tree, lays them out, handles the mouse and keyboard,
and draws them the way Blender does. The drawing code is a C port of
Blender's own widget code, and the interaction follows Blender's rules. On top
of the kit sit bindings : thin layers that let Python, Rust, JavaScript,
C++ and Dear ImGui talk to it.
What BUI is not:
Not Blender. It contains the parts of Blender's UI code it needs and
builds on its own. You don't need Blender installed, and you don't need to
know Blender to use it.
Not a browser. The Rust and JavaScript sides use HTML and CSS as a UI
language , but there's no browser engine, no webview and no network.
Not a re-imagining. The widget drawing is ported from Blender's
interface_widgets.cc , and the Dear ImGui support runs the real Dear ImGui.
2. Why BUI exists
Blender's interface is famous for how it feels . You press a number field and
drag: the cursor vanishes, the value glides under your hand, and you never hit
the edge of the screen. You type 2*pi into a field and it just works. You
type "ad cu" into a menu and it finds "Add Cube". Millions of artists have
these habits in their hands.
That interface is also fast and frugal. It redraws only what changed, sleeps
when nothing does, and starts in milliseconds. BUI exists so that any app,
in any language, can have both: Blender's feel, and Blender's efficiency.
3. Who it's for
You have a tkinter app and wish it looked less like 1998. Run it on BUI,
unchanged.
You're building a tool for artists who already know Blender. Give them
the panels, sliders and shortcuts their hands expect.
You write Rust or React and want a native desktop UI without shipping a
browser.
You use Dear ImGui and want it to look and feel like Blender, with one
build flag.
You're curious how a UI toolkit works. The source is readable, and the
concepts are explained in plain words.
Before you ship something with BUI, read the
known limitations : no accessibility support yet, no
input methods, and it looks like Blender, not like your operating system.
4. Pick your language
You can drive BUI many ways, and all of them share the same C runtime, so they
all get the same widgets and interactions:
You write
You get

5. Features at a glance
Blender's widgets and interactions
Number fields you drag with a hidden, continuous cursor : Shift for precision, Ctrl to snap.
Math in number fields , with Blender's own expression evaluator: 2*pi , min(4, 3) , round(1.7) , x if c else y .
